videos.title: Why the U.S. Navy Cannot Clear the Mines in the Strait of Hormuz
videos.description:
The U.S. Navy retired its only four mine-clearing ships from the Persian Gulf five months before this war started. Sent them to Philadelphia to be scrapped. Their replacements, billion-dollar Littoral Combat Ships, have never been proven to work. The Pentagon's own testing office says it cannot confirm the mine-clearing system is effective. Equipment works less than 30% of the time.

This video explains how naval mines actually work, why they are nearly impossible to clear quickly, how Iran turned $1,500 weapons into a $3.2 billion-per-day problem, and why even Iran itself may not know where all of its mines are.

Iran laid mines across the Strait of Hormuz starting March 10. On April 9, the IRGC published a navigational chart officially marking the international shipping lanes as a "danger zone" — the first time Iran admitted mines were in the water. All ships are now redirected to a 5-mile corridor near Larak Island, must submit full crew/cargo/ownership details to the IRGC, and pay a $1-per-barrel toll in Bitcoin or stablecoin. A standard oil tanker pays $2 million to pass through a waterway that has been free for all of recorded history.

600+ ships stranded. Oil at $109/barrel. Gas at $4.10/gallon (+37% since Feb 28). Global cost: $3.2 billion per day. The four Avenger-class ships that could clear these mines are in Sasebo, Japan — thousands of miles away. NATO allies have no minesweepers available. Timeline to clear the strait: late summer at the earliest.

In 1988, one $1,500 mine nearly sank a US warship and cost $89.5 million to repair. Iran has thousands more.

Was retiring those ships a budget decision or the most expensive cost-cutting mistake in military history?

videos.title: Why the US Navy Cannot Stop Iran's Mini Submarines?
videos.description:
Why cannot the US Navy stop Iran's mini submarines in the Strait of Hormuz? The answer is not better sonar. It is the math. At 04:11 local time this week, a steel hull about ninety-five feet long sat just below the surface of the Persian Gulf. Crew of seven. Diesel engine off. Batteries running quiet. Fourteen nautical miles north, a US Navy destroyer was on patrol. It could not hear the submarine. It could not see it. Iran has sixteen of these boats deployed right now, according to Tehran's own announcement on May 11. Each one cost less than a single F-35. And the United States Navy, which trained for decades to hunt Russian submarines in the deep Atlantic, cannot reliably find them in twenty-one miles of shallow water.

This video breaks down exactly how the Ghadir-class midget submarine, twenty-nine meters long with two torpedo tubes, holds a 2 billion dollar American destroyer at bay. We explain why the Pentagon's anti-submarine warfare playbook was written for the wrong ocean, why diesel-electric submarines on battery power are quieter than American nuclear boats, and why the institutional muscle for shallow-water sub-hunting walked out of the Navy in the early 1990s along with the retired diesel fleet.

This video also covers: how the Swedish Gotland-class submarine repeatedly sank the USS Ronald Reagan carrier strike group during 2005 exercises off California, how a Canadian Oberon-class diesel boat slipped through the screen of the USS Eisenhower in 1981 NATO exercises, why analysts Bryan Clark of the Hudson Institute and Jerry Hendrix of the Sagamore Institute have been raising the alarm for two decades, how the C-704 anti-ship missile fired from a Ghadir torpedo tube costs less than fifty thousand dollars while the American interceptor costs four million, why the Persian Gulf bottom topography defeats American sonar, and how Iran built this entire sea-denial capability for roughly two percent of the cost of the American counter-fleet.

Plus: why China is watching every move in Hormuz with the Taiwan Strait in mind, what the Yuan-class and Song-class diesel-electric submarines mean for the South China Sea, why the Three-Threat Stack of mines, drone boats, and submarines forms the new doctrine of the choke point, and the leaked CIA assessment that told the President Iran can outlast the American blockade for months, not weeks.

The Pentagon retired the Avenger-class minesweepers in September 2025. The diesel submarine fleet was retired in the early nineties. The shallow-water training command was shrunk. And Iran kept everything it had. The math of the strait has been holding for seventy-six days. Nobody in Washington has a clean answer.

This is Animated Military. We do not chase the headlines. We map the doctrine behind them.

So here is the question. Is the failure to stop the Three-Threat Stack a doctrinal collapse the Navy can still recover from, or is the Hormuz math the new permanent reality of every choke point? Write 'recover' or 'permanent' in the comments.

videos.title: China Just Sent Warships to the Gulf - Here Is What That Means for the US Blockade?
videos.description:
Three Chinese warships are sitting in the Gulf of Oman right now. Not American. Not Iranian. Chinese. And the country that buys 90% of Iran's oil just put a 30,000-ton floating supercomputer directly between the US Navy and every Iranian tanker trying to leave port. This video explains why the US naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz  which Trump activated Sunday, April 13  is no longer really a confrontation between America and Iran. It is a quiet test of resolve between Washington and Beijing, with Iran caught in the middle.

The largest Chinese ship in the Gulf is called Liaowang-1. It is not built to fight. It is built to listen. According to Defence Security Asia, its sensor bubble extends 6,000 kilometers in every direction covering the entire Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf, the Arabian Sea, and most of the Indian Ocean from a single parking position. Every American destroyer enforcing the blockade is being watched and recorded in real time. Two Chinese escorts sit beside it: a Type 055 cruiser carrying 112 missile cells and a Type 052D destroyer carrying 64.

China is not there for show. According to CNBC and Asia Times, China imports 1.4 million barrels of crude per day from Iran about 13% of total Chinese oil imports. Most of that trade is settled in yuan or cryptocurrency, bypassing the US dollar system. A decade of work by Beijing to build an alternative to dollar-denominated oil trade is now sitting on tankers stuck in Iranian ports. If the US blockade succeeds, that entire alternative system collapses on live satellite imagery from the Persian Gulf.

BBC's senior correspondent Frank Gardner put it as bluntly as any analyst has dared on television: "If there's a Chinese warship sitting off that tanker, I can't envisage a situation where you would board it. So then your blockade's failed." That is the operational reality every American destroyer captain in the strait is now navigating.

This video also covers the details nobody is connecting: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov arrived in Beijing on April 14 for two days of meetings with Wang Yi the same week the blockade went live. Russia and China just publicly reactivated their strategic partnership at the exact moment the United States needed them not to.

Plus: the casus belli scenario laid out by maritime law experts (what happens when an American boarding team climbs onto a tanker under Chinese protection), Trump's "interdict every vessel" Truth Social order targeting Chinese-flagged ships, 18 American warships in the region versus China's calibrated three-ship deployment, and the Wang Yi statement calling the blockade "dangerous and irresponsible" diplomatic language one step away from a public threat.

Brent crude is already at $103. WTI is over $104. A direct US-China naval contact in the strait even without a single shot fired would push oil past $120 in a single trading session and gasoline past $5 within weeks. All of it traces back to whether one American admiral decides to board a tanker that has a Chinese cruiser sitting beside it.

So who actually controls the Strait of Hormuz right now? Is the United States about to force this confrontation to a conclusion, or did China just neutralize the most ambitious naval operation America has run in the Middle East since the Cold War? The US destroyed over 120 Iranian naval vessels including every major warship, all three Kilo-class submarines, hundreds of fast attack boats, and hardened boat shelters along the southern coast. Iran's flagship, the Jamaran, broke apart at its own dock. One submarine was hit with an ATACMS ballistic missile. Another was torpedoed in the Indian Ocean. The A-10 Warthog, a 50-year-old plane the Air Force tried to retire, turned out to be the only cost-effective answer. videos.title: Why Iran Reopened Hormuz Then Closed It Again in 6 Hours?
videos.description:
t sunrise on April 17, Iran's foreign minister declared the Strait of Hormuz "completely open." Six hours later, Iran's parliament speaker scrapped the agreement. The Strait was closed again. The Revolutionary Guard said control had returned to its previous state. And in those six hours, oil prices crashed 11%, the S&P 500 hit an all-time record high, and the Iranian regime publicly contradicted itself in front of the entire world. This video explains exactly what happened, why Iran's own government cannot agree with itself, and why the chaos inside Tehran tells you more about the actual state of the regime than any military analysis you have read in six weeks.

The numbers tell the story. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the announcement on the morning of April 17. Within hours, US crude oil dropped from $104 to $83.85 per barrel an 11.4% crash, the second-largest single-day drop since the war began. Brent fell 9% to $90.38. The Dow jumped 1,000 points. Wall Street briefly believed the war was over.

Then came the reversal. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf publicly canceled the agreement, citing the continuing US naval blockade. The Revolutionary Guard reinforced it. Within six hours, Iran's foreign ministry had been overruled by Iran's own legislature on the most important diplomatic announcement of the war on global television. Only 5 cargo ships and 1 tanker actually crossed the Strait that day.

This video also covers: why Iran is losing $435 million per day in oil revenue and has only 13-16 days of storage capacity left before its oil fields must shut down, why the foreign minister tried to make the deal (Iran's economy is collapsing), why the Revolutionary Guard killed it (the war is the source of their domestic power), why Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir is shuttling between Tehran and Washington trying to mediate a deal Iran's own government cannot internally agree to, and why the April 22 ceasefire deadline exactly four days away could be the most consequential 96 hours of the entire war.

Plus: why Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's new supreme leader, has not been seen in public for 49 days (his face is reportedly disfigured, he has lost the use of one or both legs, and he communicates only through audio conferences), how the IDF's "we are not leaving" position on Lebanon killed Iran's attempt to link the Hormuz reopening to the Lebanon ceasefire, and the brutal institutional logic that explains why the Revolutionary Guard will refuse every deal that ends with Iran losing.

The Iranian regime, after 49 days of war, no longer has a single voice. There is a wounded supreme leader giving advice from a bunker, a foreign minister trying to make peace, a parliament speaker overruling him, and a paramilitary organization that has decided it will not accept any outcome that ends with Iran losing.

Is this the inflection point where the Iranian regime collapses from within, with America simply waiting for the inevitable? Or is this the moment when Iran becomes the most dangerous regime on earth because nobody knows who is actually making decisions for a country with thousands of ballistic missiles and the world's most important shipping lane? videos.title: Why the US Navy Cannot Stop Iran From Cutting the Global Internet?
videos.description:
Right now, every email you send, every bank transaction you process, every video you stream is moving through a cable no thicker than a garden hose, buried on the ocean floor between Iran and Oman. Seventeen of those cables carry roughly 30% of all global internet traffic. Three billion people depend on them every single day. And the most uncomfortable truth of this war is that the United States Navy, the most powerful fleet in human history, cannot actually stop Iran from cutting every one of them. This video explains which cables are at risk, why the Revolutionary Guard was built for exactly this kind of attack, and why a single Iranian combat diver with basic cutting tools could do more damage to the American economy than any missile Iran has ever fired.

The scale is hard to imagine. 95-97% of all international internet traffic moves through physical cables on the ocean floor. There is no satellite backup capable of replacing this capacity. When four cables were cut near Egypt in 2008, India's international bandwidth dropped 60% for weeks — and that was peacetime. What's at risk in the Strait of Hormuz right now is 17 cables in an active war zone: the Falcon cable (40+ terabits per second linking Mumbai to Europe), Gulf Bridge International (the backbone of seven Gulf states), Fiber in Gulf (FIG), and Meta's 45,000 km 2Africa Pearls extension designed to serve 3 billion users.

According to Bloomberg and Tom's Hardware, Meta's project is now frozen. Alcatel Submarine Networks — the French company contracted to lay the cables — officially declared force majeure and walked away. Their cable-laying ship, the Ile de Batz, is stranded off the Saudi coast. Billions of dollars in investment, suspended indefinitely.

This video also covers: the March 1 Iranian drone strikes on three Amazon Web Services data centers in the UAE and Bahrain (the first time cloud infrastructure was ever directly targeted in a conflict), the Ghadir and Fateh-class Iranian submarines built specifically for shallow-water sabotage in the Persian Gulf, the 2024 MV Rubymar incident where a single dragging anchor cut three undersea cables in the Red Sea (repairs took six months), and the fact that only 60 specialized cable repair ships exist in the entire world — and none of them can safely operate in a war zone.

Plus: why India's $250 billion IT export sector depends entirely on these cables, why American customer service, payment apps, and banking platforms would slow to a crawl if the cables go down, how Amazon, Microsoft, and Google's Gulf data centers become useless even if the buildings are intact, and why the US Navy's trained dolphin detection program — after 50+ years of service — may be one of the few tools still standing between Iran and global digital chaos.

The US Navy has not given up. P-8 Poseidon aircraft, Knifefish and Kingfish underwater drones, MH-60 Seahawk helicopters with laser mine detection — every piece of detection technology is deployed around the clock. But the Navy made a catastrophic mistake last September, retiring its four wooden-hulled Avenger-class minesweepers and replacing them with metal-hulled Littoral Combat Ships that can trigger mines themselves. Only one is currently in the Gulf. The others are thousands of miles away in Malaysia. American sailors are working with the wrong equipment to defend infrastructure nobody ever planned to defend.

Is this the defining military paradox of our time — American power so dependent on invisible digital infrastructure that a Third World regime with basic tools can hold it hostage? videos.title: 40 American Allies Just Refused to Join the US Blockade - Here Is Why
videos.description:
Forty of America's closest allies just refused to help with the Hormuz blockade. Not one or two. Forty. The United Kingdom said no first. France's president publicly called the operation "unrealistic" and warned it would get people killed. Germany, Canada, Australia, Japan, Italy, and over thirty more followed. On Friday, all forty are holding a video conference to coordinate an alternative plan for the Strait of Hormuz. The United States was not invited. This video explains why the closest military alliance in modern history just publicly broke and why this may be the most consequential moment for the Atlantic alliance since World War Two.

The numbers tell the story. Desert Storm in 1991 had 35 countries contributing forces. The Iraq war in 2003 had 46. The fight against ISIS had over 70. The Hormuz blockade in April 2026 has the United States, Israel, and a handful of Gulf partners. That is not a coalition. That is an isolation. And every dollar of the operation every gallon of fuel, every missile interceptor, every hour of sailor pay now lands on a single defense budget instead of being shared across forty allied militaries.

The UK's refusal came within hours of President Trump's April 12 announcement. French President Emmanuel Macron went further, publicly stating a military blockade of Hormuz is "not realistic" and that vessels attempting to pass through a forcibly opened strait would be "exposed to coastal threats" from Iran. In plain English, Macron told the world the blockade will get people killed and France will not be part of it. Trump responded on Truth Social: "NATO was not there for us. They will not be there for us in the future."

But Macron's position reveals something most American media is not reporting. According to Al Jazeera and Fortune, the real reason European allies refused is not philosophical it is that they believe the blockade will fail. European intelligence already knows what Institute for the Study of War reported on April 14: a sanctioned Iranian-linked tanker, the Rich Star IV, slipped through the blockade and delivered oil to China. Commercial maritime data showed 8 vessels departed Hormuz and 9 entered on April 14 the same day CENTCOM announced "zero ships" had made it through. European governments read the numbers and decided they did not want their reputations tied to a failing operation.

This video also covers: the Friday video conference that specifically excludes the United States, the 40-country alternative plan that would only begin after the American war ends, the UK's rare public break from the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's two-day visit to Beijing this week to coordinate how Russia and China exploit the NATO split, and what this split means for Taiwan, Ukraine, and every other flashpoint where American security guarantees have held the line for decades.

Brent crude is at $103. WTI is above $104. Every week the blockade runs without allied support, the full cost  estimated at tens of millions of dollars per day  lands entirely on the American taxpayer. A navy that operates alone needs more ships than one backed by allies. Every American family paying $4.13 per gallon is now also paying, indirectly, for an operation forty allies chose to sit out.

So what does this moment actually mean? Is this the historic betrayal of the American alliance by countries that happily took American protection for 75 years and refused to pay the bill when America needed something back? Or is this a reasonable decision by sensible allies who can see this operation is not worth joining? Write "betrayal" or "wisdom" in the comments.
